newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM and farmers locked in battle of wills.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM and farmers locked in battle of wills.

text.p: Prime Minister Costas Simitis was locked in a battle of wills on Tuesday with farmers blocking Greece's road and rail links for 13 days and seriously damaging the economy.
"Demands for billions (of drachmas) cannot be satisfied. To do so would be a step backwards," Simitis said after a cabinet meeting which was dominated by the farmers' protest.
The farmers, who have nearly paralysed road transport, responded by vowing to stay put until their demands were met.

"The Prime Minister's statement is a new provocation against the farmers," they said in a statement after an emergency meeting in the central city of Latissa. "We will not back down until our demands are met and our struggle vindicated."
The farmers want lower fuel prices, higher crop subsidies and a rescheduling of $1.3 billion in debts.
Simitis said in a televised statement that satisfying them would mean missing the targets set to enable Greece to play a role in the European Union.
He acknowledged that the farmers, blocking roads at 100 points with a fleet of 10,000 tractors, were creating "huge problems in the economic life of cities".
Elected to a four-year term in September and facing his first major crisis, Simitis avoided saying what he could do to free the roads -- other than wait.
Simitis's recent budget, which cuts state hiring, abolishes most tax exemptions and imposes new levies, has been pummelled by workers from a welter of industries.
The two biggest labour confederations have called a one-day nationwide strike for December 17 and many unions have declared a three-day stoppage at that time.
State doctors, teachers, public servants, customs workers and even Greek diplomats have joined in the protests, halting work, marching through Athens or staging rallies.
But the farmers are the biggest problem and they have shown no hint of compromise, setting up sprawling tent cities on the nation's highways.
"We can stay here until March when the next farming season starts. We don't have money to move the tractors anyway," said Dimitris Kelesides, an onion grower from central Larissa.
Their blockades have trapped foreign lorries from Europe, the Balkans and the Middle East for days with poor water, food and sanitation.

"The money should have been in the bank (for the trip). I'm also losing a complete journey now worth 4,000 pounds ($6,600), and I will lose the truck when I get home," British driver Bob Edwards told Reuters Television.
Drivers must stay with their trucks for fear of theft and have none of the roadside comforts which the farmers have been able to bring from nearby homes.
While the mood of the farmers is defiant, foreign truckers are despairing.
"I was hoping to be home for Christmas with my wife and family and to see everyone but I don't know if I will," David Cooper, from Manchester, England, told Reuters Television.
Simitis noted the farmers' blockades were causing chaos for many Greeks across the country as well as foreign commerce. He appeared to hope to swing public opinion against them.

"I feel like a hostage. I also want cheaper diesel but I don't go out blocking national roads. This is a Greek thing anyway and I should not pay for it," said British trucker Alan Kendall, stranded near Larissa. (1=.6047 Pound)
